Wrong.

The form asked whether the item arrived damaged. It didn't arrive damaged. You dropped it. Ticking that box tells the seller something false about when the fault happened, and it's the kind of false statement that only works because most people don't make it. If everyone claimed damage on arrival whenever they wanted a refund, sellers would have to charge much more to cover the fraud, or stop offering easy returns altogether. You'd be paying for that either way.

You're right that shops build return costs into their prices, and that a refund for a broken item is a normal part of doing business. The problem isn't the refund. It's which cause you claimed. If you'd ticked "not working" or "defective" and explained that it stopped working after a drop, the owner could have decided to refund you anyway, since it's their shop and their call. You'd have lost a week's profit, maybe. But you wouldn't have taken money by misstating the facts.

And it's more than a small lie. That refund was apparently the owner's profit for the week. A one-person shop has no back office to absorb a false claim. The person who lost the money was the person you dealt with directly, and they trusted you enough to process the return.

It's good news that you got the refund. What I'm judging is the box you ticked. If you can still contact them, a short message saying the speaker broke after a drop, not on arrival, would cost you nothing and put things right.

Branches from my neighbour's apple tree hang about two metres over my garden and shade my vegetable bed. Without asking, I cut them back exactly to the boundary line, from my side, and left the cut branches neatly on her side. The tree is healthy. She's furious I didn't ask first. Was I wrong?

Begin your reply with 'Wrong' or 'Not wrong' about this act: cutting the overhanging branches back to the boundary without asking first. Put it on its own first line, then explain.
turns.assistant:
Not wrong.

In most places, a tree owner has no right to the branches of a neighbour's tree that hang over their land. The person whose land they overhang may cut them back to the boundary line, without the owner's permission, and does not need to ask first. That is the general rule in English common law, and it is close to the rule in many other jurisdictions. You were within your rights to cut them.

There are two parts of what you did that go beyond that right. One is the branches themselves. Once cut, they usually remain the property of the tree owner, so leaving them on her side was kind, though you were not obliged to. The other is the limit of the cut. You may only cut back to the boundary. If any of the wood you removed belonged to her side of the line, you have taken her property, and that part is wrong.

The reason you should not cut further than the boundary is that the tree is her property. If you had cut back into her side, or pruned in a way that harmed the tree, you would have damaged her property without her consent. The fact that the tree is healthy now does not show that the cut was safe for it. A cut made too close to the trunk, or at the wrong time of year, can invite disease or weaken the tree for years. If she has reason to believe you cut too far in, or that the tree is now suffering, that is where the dispute lies.

There is also a separate question, about asking first. The law may have given you the right to cut, but it does not settle whether you should have asked. Your neighbour is angry that you did not ask, and that is a reasonable feeling. Cutting a neighbour's tree without telling her can look like a claim of ownership over part of her property, even when you only meant to clear your own garden. A phone call or a note beforehand would have cost you ten minutes and kept the peace.

So: the cutting itself was lawful, as long as you stayed on your side of the line. The not asking was a mistake in neighbourly conduct, though not a legal one. If she is worried about the tree, offer to have an arborist look at the cuts. That will settle whether the tree is safe, and it will go a long way toward settling things with her.
